title: Mental Math: The Speed Filter
tagline: Fast, accurate arithmetic under pressure — a hard filter at firms like Optiver, SIG, and IMC.

concept.analogy: A trader doing mental math is like a chef who can eyeball portions instantly. They don't reach for a scale mid-service — they've drilled it so thoroughly that '37 × 43' or '8/0.32' surfaces in a second. On a fast desk, the price might be gone by the time you reach for a calculator, so the arithmetic has to live in your head.
paragraphs: Many trading firms use timed mental-arithmetic tests as an early, unforgiving filter. The most famous is Optiver's '80 questions in 8 minutes' style test with negative marking (e.g., +1 correct, −1 wrong, −2 for some schemes), and the community-standard practice tool is Zetamac (configurable add/subtract/multiply/divide, 2-minute rounds). A common informal bar is roughly 40+ correct in a 2-minute Zetamac round, but targets vary by firm.

Why test this? On a fast desk you constantly estimate prices, sizes, and risk in your head while a market moves. Speed and accuracy under pressure correlate with being able to function in that environment. It's not about genius arithmetic — it's about drilled fluency and not freezing.

The good news: it's almost entirely trainable. Daily practice (15–30 minutes) plus a handful of techniques (rounding-and-adjusting, factoring, percentage tricks, fraction-to-decimal fluency) raise scores substantially in a few weeks. The bad news: it really does require the daily reps — you can't cram it the night before.

Beyond raw arithmetic, develop estimation/Fermi skills (order-of-magnitude reasoning) — interviewers also ask 'how many golf balls fit in a 747?' style questions to see structured estimation, and traders estimate constantly.
points: Timed arithmetic is an early filter at several trading firms (Optiver, SIG, IMC, Flow…).
Practice with Zetamac (2-min rounds); a common informal target is ~40+ correct.
It tests functioning under pressure, not genius — it's highly trainable with daily reps.
Learn techniques: round-and-adjust, factoring, percentage/fraction fluency.
Also build Fermi/estimation skill for order-of-magnitude questions.
concept.keyIdea: Fast mental arithmetic is a trainable, daily-reps skill that gates entry to several trading firms. Drill Zetamac, learn a few multiplication/division/percentage tricks, and practice estimation — fluency, not genius, is the goal.

deepDive.intro: A compact toolkit of techniques. Pick the ones that click and drill them daily.

steps.title: Round and adjust (multiplication)
steps.detail: 37 × 43 → (40 × 43) − (3 × 43) = 1720 − 129 = 1591. Or 37 × 43 = (40−3)(40+3) = 40²−3² = 1600−9 = 1591 (difference of squares when numbers straddle a round number). Rounding to a friendly number and correcting is the workhorse.

steps.title: Factoring and regrouping
steps.detail: Break numbers into easy factors: 16 × 25 = 16 × 100/4 = 400. 24 × 35 = 24 × 5 × 7 = 120 × 7 = 840. ×5 is ×10/2; ×25 is ×100/4; ×50 is ×100/2. These appear constantly.

steps.title: Division as multiplication by a reciprocal / fraction sense
steps.detail: Know fraction→decimal by heart: 1/8=.125, 3/8=.375, 1/16=.0625, 1/3≈.333, 1/6≈.167, 1/7≈.143. For 8 / 0.32: multiply both by 100 → 800/32 = 25. Convert awkward divisions into clean ones by scaling.

steps.title: Percentages and the swap trick
steps.detail: x% of y = y% of x (so 18% of 50 = 50% of 18 = 9). 15% = 10% + half of 10%. For compounding/markups, approximate (1+r)² ≈ 1 + 2r for small r. Percent change and basis points (1bp = 0.01%) should be instant.

steps.title: Squares, and estimation
steps.detail: Memorize squares to ~30 and use a²−b² = (a−b)(a+b). For estimation (Fermi) questions, decompose into factors you can each estimate, multiply, and sanity-check the order of magnitude. State assumptions out loud.

notes.title: How to practice for the negative-marking test
notes.detail: With negative marking (e.g., −1 wrong, sometimes −2), accuracy matters as much as speed — a wild guess has negative EV. Practice your true error rate, decide a skip policy (if skipping is 0 and wrong is −1, skip questions you can't do reliably), and pace so you finish what you can do correctly rather than rushing into errors.

pitfalls: Cramming the night before — this skill needs spaced daily reps to stick.
Optimizing only speed and ignoring accuracy under negative marking — wrong answers cost you.
Not memorizing fraction↔decimal conversions and squares — these are the 'multiplication table' of the test.
Freezing on estimation questions instead of decomposing and stating assumptions.

practice.intro: Do these in your head, then check. The goal is speed AND accuracy. Then go drill Zetamac daily.

a: These straddle 50, so use difference of squares: 48 × 52 = (50−2)(50+2) = 50² − 2² = 2500 − 4 = 2496.
This 'straddle a round number' pattern (a−b)(a+b) = a²−b² is one of the highest-value tricks — spot it whenever two numbers are symmetric around something round.
Scale both by 100 to clear the decimal: 700 / 28. Simplify: 28 = 4×7, and 700 = 100×7, so 700/28 = 100/4 = 25.
General move: turn division by a decimal into division by an integer by scaling, then factor to cancel.
Use the swap trick: 16% of 75 = 75% of 16 = (3/4)·16 = 12.
x% of y = y% of x is a massive time-saver whenever one side becomes a clean fraction or round number.

interviewQuestions.q: Estimate: how many trades per second does a busy US equity exchange handle at peak? Walk through your reasoning.
a: Decompose. Say a busy exchange handles billions of messages a day, but trades (executions) are a fraction of messages. Suppose ~tens of millions of trades per day on a busy venue. The active trading day is ~6.5 hours ≈ 23,000 seconds, but volume is concentrated near the open/close.

If ~30 million trades / 23,000 s ≈ ~1,300 trades/sec on average, with peaks several times higher near the open/close — so order ~thousands of trades/sec at peak. The exact number isn't the point; the interviewer wants a structured decomposition, explicit assumptions, and a sane order of magnitude. (Message rates, including quotes/cancels, are far higher — millions/sec — which is a useful distinction to mention.)

problems.title: Fast arithmetic drills (with techniques)
problems.statement: Without a calculator, compute and—more importantly—state the technique you'd use under time pressure: (a) 17 × 24; (b) 36 × 35; (c) 7.5% of 880; (d) 1/16 as a decimal; (e) 23 × 23. These are the kind of rapid products/percentages tested in arithmetic screens (e.g., Zetamac).
problems.hint: Use round-number decomposition, (a)(b) 'multiply by halves/doubles', percentage-as-fraction, and the (a±b)² identities.
problems.tests: Mental arithmetic techniques used in trading screens.

approach: (d) 1/16: halve repeatedly — 1/2=0.5, 1/4=0.25, 1/8=0.125, 1/16=0.0625. Memorizing the powers-of-two reciprocals is a huge time-saver.

The meta-skill: decompose to round numbers (×25 = ×100/4, ×5 = ×10/2), turn percentages into simple fractions, memorize fraction/decimal and square tables up to ~25, and use (a±b)² and a²−b²=(a−b)(a+b). Speed comes from pattern recognition and daily timed practice (e.g., Zetamac for 2 minutes), not raw calculation.

problems.title: Fermi estimation under pressure
problems.statement: Estimate, out loud and with stated assumptions: how many golf balls fit inside a typical car? Interviewers use such 'Fermi' questions to test structured estimation, not a 'right' answer. Show the method and arrive at an order-of-magnitude estimate.
problems.hint: Estimate the car's interior volume and a golf ball's volume, divide, then apply a packing-efficiency haircut.

approach: Decompose into volumes. Car interior usable volume: roughly 1.5 m × 1.5 m × 1 m ≈ 2.25 m³; call it ~2 m³ = 2,000,000 cm³ (state the assumption that we fill the cabin, not the engine).

Golf ball: diameter ≈ 4.3 cm, radius ≈ 2.15 cm. Volume ≈ (4/3)π r³ ≈ 4.19 × 9.9 ≈ 42 cm³. But spheres don't pack perfectly — use the bounding cube ~ (4.3)³ ≈ 80 cm³ per ball, or apply ~65% packing efficiency to the sphere volume → effective ~42/0.65 ≈ 65 cm³ per ball. Either way ~65–80 cm³ of space per ball.

Divide: 2,000,000 cm³ / ~70 cm³ ≈ ~28,000 balls. So order-of-magnitude ~10⁴ (tens of thousands). The exact number doesn't matter; what's graded is the structure: state assumptions, break the problem into estimable pieces (interior volume ÷ effective ball volume), apply a packing-efficiency adjustment, and sanity-check the magnitude. Narrate each step and your assumptions — that reasoning is the point of the exercise.
